1:
Barnes reads the chapter as an episode deliberately placed for relief: the two preceding chapters had described woes threatening to destroy the church, and it was proper that the gloomy picture be broken by symbols holding out ultimate and certain victory. The others catch the contrast in the imagery itself. Bede sets the two standing-places against each other, the beast on the sand of the sea and the Lamb on Mount Zion, and says the church is shown rejoicing in its wonted splendour and numbers so that no one should fear the body of the Lamb had succumbed to the fury of the beast. Henry works the same antithesis through the animal: a counterfeit lamb had risen out of the earth in the previous chapter which was really a dragon, whereas here is the true paschal Lamb, so that the mediatorial government is the fruit of his sufferings. Ellicott presses the article, that it is the Lamb and not a lamb, and sets Zion against the Babylon about to be introduced. Robertson locates the mountain as the site of the new city, and observes that the name on their foreheads stands where the mark of the beast stood, the seal protecting them.

On the number Bede offers an arithmetic. The finite figure ought to be understood as infinite and as suited to the virgin band which loves God with the whole heart, soul and mind, and to the body which consists of four qualities; for three times three is nine and four times four is sixteen, and sixteen nines make a hundred and forty-four. Ellicott takes the number as representing the full growth of the choice ones of God, the true Israel; Robertson notes that some scholars seek a distinction between this company and the sealed of the earlier vision, though he refers them to the same. On the song, Ellicott corrects the rendering and probably the text, giving they sing rather than they sung as it were, and assigns it to the heavenly harpers before the throne; Robertson observes that in the earlier vision the new song was sung by the living creatures and the elders while here it is sung before them, apparently by the redeemed themselves. What it means that no one else could learn it is answered alike by three. Barnes says none who had not been redeemed could enter into the feelings of those who were; Clarke that others cannot know why believers exult so much; Wesley more narrowly, that they could not sing and play it in the same manner.

Whether the undefiled are literally so divides the readers four ways. Barnes takes the word for defiled as determining the sense and reads plain chastity, while denying that the passage may be pressed further. Clarke and Gill both make it idolatry, Clarke reading them as pure from idols and presented as unspotted virgins to their Saviour, with a possible allusion to Israel's sin through the Midianite women, and Gill identifying the defilement with the wine of the harlot's fornication. Wesley treats it as part put for the whole, the deepest defilement standing for every other, so that virgins means unspotted souls who have preserved universal purity. Robertson lays out the scholarship without settling it: the noun can be applied to men as well as women, one commentator takes the language metaphorically as the symbolic character of the book suggests, another judges it an interpolation in the interest of celibacy, and a third holds that taken literally it can refer only to adultery or fornication; Robertson himself insists that since the New Testament exalts marriage the passage should not be construed as degrading it. On the mouth without guile, Robertson notes that where a prophet had written lie an apostle quoting him wrote deceit, and thinks the difference small.
6:
Who the flying angel is draws the widest spread of answers in the chapter. Gill denies it is one of the ministering spirits at all, since the preaching of the gospel is committed to none of them, and takes it for a set of gospel ministers; he canvasses the eighth and ninth century opponents of image worship and rejects them because little of the everlasting gospel was preached then, and moves on to the forerunners of the Reformation, naming Wycliffe in England, Petrarch in Italy and Huss. Clarke declines to choose between a dispensation of providence, an order of preachers and a society, and then identifies the vision with something in his own lifetime, the British and Foreign Bible Society, whose object is to print and circulate the Scriptures in all the languages spoken on earth; he lists the tongues already served. Wesley makes the three angels of this passage three men bringing messages from God. Barnes takes another to mean simply a further one in a series John had grown used to seeing, and reads the vision's design as identical with the previous one, to sustain the courage of a persecuted church by the assurance that the gospel would ultimately triumph. Henry says only that such work is fit for an angel.

Robertson presses the wording and finds it careful. This is the only occurrence of the noun for gospel anywhere in the writer's works, and it stands without the article, so that what is proclaimed is not the gospel but a proclamation of God's eternal purpose; the adjective for everlasting appears nowhere else in the book though it is common in the fourth gospel and the first epistle. He notes that Origen took the eternal gospel here to be another book still to be written. Wesley reaches the same conclusion by a plainer route, that it is not the gospel properly so called but a joyful message meant to have influence on all ages. Ellicott by contrast treats it as the gospel outright, the good news that God loves the world and has redeemed mankind, and calls it the sword of the Spirit put into an angel's hand and raised in view of all nations. Henry takes everlasting in two senses at once, of its nature and of its consequences, since all flesh is grass but the word of the Lord endures. Robertson also observes the grammatical seam, that the participle for having agrees with the angel while the participle for saying in the next verse shifts to the nominative as though a new sentence began.

The summons itself is read as anti-idolatrous by everyone who comments on it. Barnes calls it the substance of the gospel, its end and design being to turn men from every form of idol worship and superstition to the only true God, and reads the judgment clause as pointing to the same solemn scene Daniel had described. Clarke says the same in a sentence, that the true God is to be worshipped and glory given to him because to him alone and not to idols or men all glory belongs. Wesley draws the practical consequence, that those who fear God and give him glory will not worship the beast nor any image whatever, and notes that the four things named as made by the Creator are precisely the objects on which the vials are afterwards poured. Ellicott hears the summons as addressed to people sitting inactive on the earth who must be roused, and answers the question when this angel appeared by saying the whole cycle of gospel preaching is included in the vision, though some ages have seen the light go forth with revived lustre. Robertson notes that it is a call to judgment with no hope offered except by implication, and that the verb for worship takes the dative.
8:
What Babylon stands for is the question, and the answers run from a single city to a principle. Barnes proceeds by abstraction: the literal Babylon was chiefly remembered by the Hebrews as the power that invaded the holy land, ruined the temple, reduced the country to a province and carried the people into captivity, so that the name became an emblem of everything haughty and oppressive and especially of whatever persecutes the church; the word must therefore denote here some later power resembling it in those characteristics. Clarke reports that Rome is called Babylon in the rabbinical writings, along with the titles the great city and great Rome, then asks which Rome is meant, pagan or papal, and answers only that some parts of the description apply best to the former. Robertson says flatly that Rome is meant and adds the circumstance that explains the veil, since a prisoner on Patmos could speak his mind only by such symbolism. Ellicott refuses to fix it to one age at all: pagan Rome was Babylon to the seer, papal Rome to a later age, and Babylon has reared palaces on the Seine and the Thames as well as the Tiber and the Bosphorus, so that she is an emblem of principles all nations have accepted in some measure.

Wesley dates her instead. Rome commenced Babylon, he says, when it commenced the great city, that is when it swallowed the Grecian monarchy and its fragments and so obtained dominion over Jerusalem some sixty years before the nativity; her spiritual greatness began in the fifth century and increased from age to age, and will reach its height just before the overthrow. He notes that the epithet great is added wherever the name occurs, and reads the whole as a parallel: what Babylon was to the Israel of old, Rome has been to the literal and the spiritual Israel alike, so that as the liberty of the ancient Jews was bound up with the fall of the Babylonish empire, the liberty of God's people waits on the fall of Rome. Gill turns the same expectation into a sequence of preachers, offering the Waldenses and Albigenses, who laid a foundation for her ruin, and Luther and his fellow reformers, who gave her a deadly blow so that she has been falling ever since, before settling on a body of ministers still to come who will live to declare her actual fall. Ellicott puts the sequence the other way about, that the principles of the gospel undermine the world-power, so that the fall of some Babylon principle has almost always followed an age of revival.

Robertson hears the doubled verb as a dirge announcing the certainty of the fall, prefers the English participial rendering as more musical than the literal one, and traces the echo to Isaiah, noting that one Greek witness there has the perfect instead. He derives the phrase that follows from Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon combined with two other passages in this book, and pictures Rome as the great courtesan who intoxicates and beguiles the nations while the cup of wrath stands full for her and her paramours. Clarke explains the image from a practice rather than a text, that impure women gave love potions to those they wished to bind to their will, generally intoxicating in nature, inflaming the blood and disturbing the intellect, so that the wine of wrath is the envenomed cup given by such women; he adds that no nation spread its idolatries so widely as the ancient Romans, whose worship went as far as their conquests. Wesley identifies the fornication with idolatry, the invocation of saints, the worship of images and human traditions, holding that fleshly fornication is joined to the spiritual abundantly, and observes pointedly that the making of the nations drink is ascribed not to the beast but to Babylon herself.
9:
The threatened cup is read as a judicial one. Barnes takes the image from the practice of holding out poison to a condemned man to drink and die, and explains unmixed as undiluted with water, that is at full strength, so that the punishment is unmitigated. Clarke makes the same allusion to the poisoned cup certain criminals were obliged to drink, on which speedy death followed, and reads the sentence as retributive: having drunk the intoxicating wine of spiritual fornication they now drink the wine of God's wrath. Gill notes that the phrase wine of wrath is one the Jewish writers use. Robertson finds a bold and powerful oxymoron in the Greek, since the participle means mixed and the adjective means unmixed, so that the phrase reads the mixed unmixed: the wine is unmixed with water yet mixed with spices to make it stronger still. He distinguishes the two nouns for anger that stand side by side elsewhere, one vehement fury and the other settled indignation, and says the white heat held back through the ages will be turned loose. Clarke hears in fire and brimstone an allusion to the punishment of Sodom, and takes the angels and the Lamb as the instruments of the destruction rather than mere spectators.

On the duration they diverge, and the divergence is instructive. Gill takes it plainly, that there will be no end to the torment, and cites the Jewish phrase about the smoke of hell filling the eyes of the wicked. Barnes is more guarded about what the words strictly prove: the clause affirms only that the smoke of their torment ascends, which does not by itself assert that the individual sufferings are eternal, though it is such language as would be used on that supposition and can hardly be explained otherwise. Ellicott moves the question onto moral ground, reading the restlessness as the natural consequence of sin, which is first embraced as a delight and soon becomes an inexorable tyrant compelling men along habits they loathe while they long for them, so that there is a destiny of unrest in all sin. Robertson notes that the phrase for having no rest is the very language used earlier of the living creatures praising God, and quotes the judgement that those who desert Christ for Caesar become victims of a remorse that never dies or sleeps. Wesley writes only that God grant we may never try the strict literal eternity of this torment. Barnes and Clarke both trace the ascending smoke to the overthrow of Sodom.

Wesley uses the passage to strike at a doctrine rather than to expound one. Having called this the most terrible threatening in all Scripture, and observed that God arms his servants against the fear of the beast by a greater fear, he asks whether no real anger is implied in all this, and exclaims at what even wise men will assert in order to serve a hypothesis. On the closing verse the readings differ mainly in grammar and emphasis. Ellicott corrects the rendering, so that it runs here is the patience of the saints who keep, not here are they that keep, and locates the patience in the readiness to wait and endure to the end. Robertson notes the same construction as an anacoluthon frequent in this book, and reads the whole as the writer's own comment on a struggle against emperor worship that tested loyalty to Christ. Barnes offers two senses, that those who show such patience prove themselves God's children, or that the disclosure about the persecutors' end is itself designed to sustain them. Clarke suggests the word sometimes means the reward of perseverance rather than the virtue, so that the verse promises blessedness to those who die for the testimony.
13:
The command to write is taken as a mark of weight. Barnes suggests the seer had been recording what he saw and is now told to record what he heard, and offers the verse as evidence that the book was written as the disclosures were made rather than afterwards from memory. Wesley notes that the command had already been given for the whole book, so that wherever it is repeated it marks something peculiarly observable, and guesses the voice belonged to a departed saint; he adds that the word is heard most seasonably when the beast is at the height of his power and fury. Robertson says the meditation is broken by the command, and that this beatitude for the Christian dead goes further than what the apostle had written to the Thessalonians and Corinthians. Clarke reads the solemnity the same way, that information of the utmost importance is communicated by a voice from heaven. Ellicott observes that we are not told whose voice speaks, and insists the blessing covers not only martyrs but all who die in happy union and fellowship with their Lord. Henry values the prophecy for coming down from heaven and not from men, which makes it of certain truth and great authority.

Clarke alone sets the saying beside its pagan analogues. Happy are the dead, he says, is a proverb frequently met with in the Greek and Roman poets, and he quotes the Odyssey, where the shipwrecked man calls thrice and four times happy those who fell at Troy and wishes he had died on that well fought field, and then the Latin imitation, where the hero's limbs loosen with cold and he stretches both palms to the stars with the same cry. Clarke divides the happiness of the Christian dead into two things which the pagan proverb reaches only in part: they do not see the evil coming on the world and are exempt from further suffering, and they actually enjoy blessedness. Wesley gives the same two reasons for the words from henceforth, that they escape the approaching calamities and already enjoy so near an approach to glory. Ellicott finds those words a difficulty and offers the state of trouble just described as the reason for them, the righteous being happy in being taken from the evil to come, before suggesting a second use, that they may console mourners in an age whose unbelief writes farewell for ever over its graves. Robertson attaches the phrase instead to those who die in the Lord.

On the rest and the works that follow, three of them guard the same point in almost the same words. Henry says the works do not go before as a title or price of purchase but follow as evidence of having lived and died in the Lord; Wesley says they do not go before to procure admittance into the mansions of joy but follow when admittance is given, and specifies that what follows is the fruit of the works, each one's peculiar works. Ellicott makes them works of faith and labours of love, even the giving of a cup of cold water in Christ's name, following with them into the presence of their Lord. Robertson draws the distinction the Greek makes, that they rest from their toils and wearinesses but not from their activities, since those follow with them; heaven is not a place of idleness but of the highest form of spiritual service, so that growth cut short here can be utilised there. Henry lists what the rest is rest from: sin, temptation, sorrow and persecution. Wesley marks the contrast sharply, that no pain and no purgatory follows, that the more laborious the life the sweeter the rest, and that this state is the opposite of those two verses earlier who have no rest day or night.
14:
The figure on the cloud is identified the same way by everyone who takes it up, and Gill does it by elimination: not some great prince who encouraged the Reformation among his subjects, nor an angel in human shape, nor Martin Luther as others have said, but Christ himself. Ellicott builds the identification from four converging marks, the cloud, the title son of man, the crown, and the general resemblance to the opening vision of the book; Barnes finds a designed reference to Daniel; Robertson lists the passages where the same cloud appears and calls it a familiar object in Mediterranean lands. Clarke reads the crown as a token of victory and regal power, Ellicott as the crown of conquest with the hour at hand, and Robertson distinguishes it from the diadems worn later, this being a wreath. On the two images that govern the rest of the chapter, Clarke says harvest and vintage were frequent among the ancient prophets for the destruction of nations, and Henry separates their objects: the harvest gathers the righteous when ripe for heaven, the vintage destroys the enemies of Christ once their sin has ripened them for ruin, since the patience of God towards sinners is the greatest miracle in the world but will not be everlasting.

Barnes numbers the angels as they come, the fourth crying to the reaper, the fifth carrying the second sickle, the sixth calling for the vintage, and insists on the direction of the command in the first case: it is not the angel's order but the Father's, borne by the angel to the Son, which agrees with the whole New Testament representation that the Messiah is subordinate in the work given him to do. Robertson agrees that the angel urges Christ, and notes the urgency in the aorist imperatives; he takes the verb rendered ripe as meaning dried up or withered, and doubts the sense over-ripe. On the angel from the altar, Robertson gives the alternatives and their consequences: if it is the altar of burnt offering we are reminded of the blood of the martyrs, if the altar of incense then of the prayers of the saints. Clarke identifies him with the angel of an earlier chapter who stood by the altar with authority over its fire; Ellicott holds both earlier scenes in view at once, the souls beneath the altar and the angel who flung the burning ashes earthward. Gill reports without endorsing an interpretation that made these two angels Thomas Cromwell and Archbishop Cranmer and the vintage the dissolution of the religious houses.

The measured distance at the close draws the widest guesses. Barnes computes it as two hundred miles and treats it as a lake of blood standing for a great slaughter, without pressing the figure. Wesley takes it as the length of Palestine, at least two hundred miles, and marks the depth as deep at its first flowing. Robertson allows that the distance does cover the length of the land but thinks it more likely that the metaphor is worked out with the exuberance of apocalyptic symbolism. Clarke alone finds a modern coincidence, reporting that the papal state extends from Rome to the Po, two hundred Italian miles, which make exactly sixteen hundred furlongs, and calling the correspondence surprising and worthy of deep regard; he also supplies the Jewish hyperbole that when Hadrian besieged a certain city he slew so many that the horses waded in blood up to their mouths. On the place, Barnes notes that a winepress stood in the vineyard rather than in a city and that the vision shows it outside the walls; Robertson recalls that this was the usual place and that a prophet had made the valley of Jehoshaphat the scene of the slaughter of God's enemies; Gill mentions the suggestion that the olive presses outside Jerusalem gave Gethsemane its name.
